$comment: Which exemplar page demonstrates which decorator options. Every option in the SDK surface must be claimed by exactly one page, or explicitly deferred. A page may claim options across several decorators when they teach one concept. Options are written as LITERALS in the exemplar source - never Storybook args - so the extracted snippet is the lesson.
$provenance: Option side: decorator-surface-full.json, extracted mechanically from SDK source. Page grouping: the concept organisation of the previous codex (futures, state-machine, config-property, container-models, topic-handlers, event-bus...). This is a STARTING POINT, not a fixed plan - validate each page against kos://decorator/* and kos://guide/* and change what does not hold up.

kosReference.reason: Believed not to work as documented; excluded until the behaviour is confirmed.

kosModel.reason: Being deprecated. Auto-registration is a hack with many failure modes; models are registered explicitly in the app's registration chain. The codex must not teach it as a normal option.

kosSubscribe.reason: Marked @deprecated and @internal in SDK source (kosSubscribe.ts: warnDeprecated → replacement @kosTopicHandler, removeAt 3). The codex must not teach a decorator scheduled for removal.

kosTopicHandler.reason: Marked @internal in IKosTopicHandlerParams; they select the FOS broker transport, which needs a FOS-capable device and cannot be demonstrated against KosMock.

kosServiceRequest.reason: queryParams: none of the Studio endpoints the codex uses declares query parameters, and the typed decorator rejects untyped ones. extensions: declared in IKosServiceRequestParams but no code path in the request manager reads it (verified in SDK source), so nothing can be demonstrated.

kosContainerAware.reason: containerOptions.parentId is inferred from the owning model's id; legacy switches the container property to the pre-decorator `_models` name. includeGetters and includeMethods default to true and are only meaningful as false, to keep the decorator from injecting members a class already defines. All four are migration controls the codex leaves out.

kosStateProp.reason: Binds to the device State service (/api/kos/state). The codex runs against the codex backend, whose OpenAPI has no state service (checked: no /api/state paths), so nothing can be projected.

kosStateBean.reason: Same as kosStateProp: no state service on the codex backend.

kosParentAware.reason: Names a non-default option key for the parent id; exists for options shapes from legacy code. New models use the default kosParentId and let the container set the parent, so the codex does not demonstrate it.

kosCompanion.reason: Only read in decorator mode (it lists parent members not to proxy). The codex's companion is a composition companion, so there is no honest home for it.

pages.teaches: The minimum model: a type id, a lifecycle, and where registration actually happens.
How models compose into a system: dependency (read a model you do not own) and containment (own children) as the two primary relationships, with context, parent awareness and companions.
The ways a model talks to the backend, each a decorator: service requests, topics, configuration properties, futures, troubles (state beans deferred); which to use when.
A computed model property derives from other properties, including models injected by @kosDependency, so a model consumes another model's state and reacts to it without owning it.

A PropKey ({MODEL_ID} or createPropKey) makes a decorator option read a model property per instance: topic paths, service request params, dependency ids and options. The options themselves are claimed by the Topic Handlers and Model Dependencies pages; this page teaches the substitution.

websocket:true subscribes the method to transport frames; websocket:false subscribes it to the in-app EventBus. lifecycle picks the phase that registers the subscription. skipParse (marked @internal) hands over the unparsed body.
Narrowing which frames reach a handler, reshaping the payload, and handlers that fire exactly once.
Side by side: debounce hands the handler an ARRAY of the quiet window, throttle keeps one frame per window, buffer bounds by size or time. They are mutually exclusive: one wrapper per handler.
The flow object is a separate pipeline from the top-level shortcuts: transform sees raw frames, a partial batch waits for the next event, rateLimit drops rather than throttles.

Both halves of not missing frames: hold a delta handler until the baseline request on the same path has answered (and replay what queued meanwhile), and keep the last frames on a topic for late subscribers.
Trailing-wildcard subscriptions with a named capture, and addressing a subscription to a specific destination.
A container owns a collection and the events that change it, and what the decorator injects can be renamed or trimmed.
Indexes make a container queryable without scanning; property-based and function-based forms.
Capacity as a safety net: the container evicts and destroys overflow, and fifo, lru or a custom filter decide what goes.
A declarative service request, and the error-first tuple it returns.
Turning a response payload into models without hand-written mapping code.
Response caching, and what extendOnRefresh changes about expiry.
Failure policy declared with the request instead of repeated at every call site.
A long-running device operation as one awaitable future with a phase stream, plus cancellation and what trackerPolicy counts as still running.
Why concurrent operations need the multiple-future form: a single futureAware shares one slot, so two calls collide.
Binding a model field to device configuration, binding a whole subtree, and what lazy defers.
Unit conversion and display formatting at the binding, not in the view.
Declaring a dependency on another model, which lifecycle phase resolves it, and optionsRequired: the dependency target's guard against being created with no options.
Reaching the owning model, and what child lifecycle ownership means for cleanup.
Attaching behaviour to a model you do not own.
Lifecycle as an explicit machine with entry and exit hooks; throwOnInvalid lives on the guard, not on the machine config.
Reacting to a change without a topic, and whether the effect runs on registration.
A model shaped for a view rather than for the device.
Surfacing device faults through a model.
Per-model logging with a named context, and grouping the output of one method.
What the creation context carries, and what the framework calls on reload - a model never calls reload itself.
The options that exist for migration, special shapes or specific situations, each with the use case that justifies it and the page that shows it; none is a default to reach for.
